entrypoints.summary: An attacker submits POST /forgot-password with a target username and an X-Forwarded-Host header accepted by the application.

negative_controls: No separately executed control condition is supplied by the lab source.
observability.positive_marker: A GET /forgot-password request includes the victim token as a query parameter, followed by successful login using the new Carlos password.

preconditions: The victim Carlos clicks links received by email, as stipulated by the lab.
The attacker can submit a password-reset request with an X-Forwarded-Host header and can observe requests to an attacker-controlled exploit server.
A valid reset URL structure is available so the captured token can be substituted.

trigger_steps.summary: Observe the victim's token in the exploit-server request and place it in a valid reset URL to set a new Carlos password.

sources.concept: Attacker-controlled forwarded host header in password-reset request

impact.affected_asset: Carlos's account and its password-reset credential/token.
impact.attacker_capability: Obtain the victim reset token after the victim follows the poisoned email link, reset the victim password, and authenticate as the victim.
impact.security_effect: Account takeover through capture and reuse of a victim's password-reset token.

causal_trace.summary: The password-reset request accepts the X-Forwarded-Host header, which the lab states can point a dynamically generated reset link to an arbitrary domain.
The origin embedded in an emailed password-reset URL is no longer bound to a trusted application-controlled reset origin; it is selected from attacker-controlled forwarded-host input.

When a reset is requested for Carlos, the application sends an email link containing a unique reset token but with the attacker-selected host; Carlos following it produces a GET to the attacker domain with the token in a query parameter.
The attacker can substitute the captured victim token into a valid reset URL, set a new password, and log in to Carlos's account.

failure.operation: Dynamic construction of the emailed reset-link origin from supported X-Forwarded-Host input

primary_invariant.statement: A password-reset email must contain a token-bearing URL whose origin is a trusted application-controlled reset origin, rather than an origin derived from requester-controlled forwarding headers.
primary_invariant.violated_because: The documented lab behavior supports X-Forwarded-Host and uses it to direct the dynamically generated reset link to an arbitrary domain.

quality.review_notes: This is a PortSwigger training-lab exemplar, not evidence of prevalence or a versioned production defect. The source documents an exploit sequence and outcome but supplies neither application source nor a remediation patch. The negative condition and remediation are invariant-derived rather than documented as a tested fix; no execution result is claimed.

remediation.invariant_restored: Generate reset URLs from a configured trusted origin and do not allow requester-controlled X-Forwarded-Host values to select the token-bearing link destination.
mitigation_classes: forwarded-host allowlisting or rejection for reset-link generation

affected_versions_or_commits.value: Lab content observed 2026-07-16; no product version or commit is supplied.

target.component: Forgot-password endpoint and dynamically generated email reset link
target.project_or_package: PortSwigger Web Security Academy password-reset-poisoning lab application

oracle.channel: HTTP request, exploit-server access log, and authentication outcome
oracle.expected_negative: With reset-link origin integrity enforced, an attacker-provided X-Forwarded-Host must not cause a victim reset token to be sent in a request to the attacker domain.
oracle.expected_positive: In the vulnerable lab flow, a POST /forgot-password for Carlos carrying an attacker exploit-server X-Forwarded-Host results in a logged GET request containing Carlos's reset token; using that token in a valid reset URL permits setting a new password and logging in as Carlos.
